newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus political opponents avert clash with deal.
newsitem.headline: Belarus political opponents avert clash with deal.

text.p: Political opponents in Belarus signed a compromise deal on Friday to resolve a standoff between President Alexander Lukashenko and the parliament that had threatened stability in the former Soviet republic.
Reporters watched as Lukashenko, Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Belarus parliamentary speaker Semyon Sharetksy and the speakers of Russia's two houses of parliament signed the agreement.

Lukashenko said he had agreed that the results of a controversial referendum set for Sunday on extending his presidential powers would not be binding. In return, parliament would not try to impeach him.

"This is a very important step. In simple terms, it marks an the end to confrontation that the Belarus people have been waiting for," said Chernomyrdin, who flew from Moscow on an 11th hour mission to help defuse the crisis.
Chernomyrdin admitted that the talks, which dragged on for more than five hours, had been tough.
"Yes, the negotiations were very difficult," he said. "I have not been involved in such an undertaking for 15 years."
The chairman of parliament, Semyon Sharetsky, said that Russia had helped bring about a deal acceptable to both sides.

"No one won and no one lost. We sought and won a sensible copmpromise," he said. "We could have come to this compromise ourselves but with the Russian participation it was easier and there was a guarantee."
Chernomyrdin said that a political treaty signed between Russia and Belarus meant that Moscow felt closely connected to the fate of its neighbour.
"We also carry responsibility for the agreement which has been signed," he said, but he emphasised that Russia took part only as mediator and did not force the deal.
Lukashenko said that under the deal the opposing political forces would work together on a new constitution, taking into account the results of Sunday's referendum.
"Over 20 days a constitutional committee will be created -- containing 50 representatives each of parliament and of the president -- which will confirm the final make-up of a new constitution."

"The committee will be headed by the president. The committee must over three months accept a new constitution on the basis of whatever draft is accepted by a majority in the referendum," Lukashenko said.
The constitutional court, which had been due to rule on the opposition's impeachment moves later on Friday, would drop the case, he added.
"Until a new constitution is accepted there can be no talk of either the impeachment of the president or the dissolution of parliament," Lukashenko said.
